To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) MRS and NIRS can be used to assess cerebral oxidative metabolism in newborn infants; (2) MRS identifies delayed failure of cerebral energy metabolism in newborn infants after pernital asphyxia; (3) Haemodynamic abnormalities precede the delayed reduction in energy metabolism in asphyxiated newborn infants.
MRS and NIRS can be used to assess cerebral oxidative metabolism in newborn infants and to detect derangements of energy metabolism following hypoxic-ischaemic insult.
NIRS and MIRS are useful tools in assessing the brain of the newborn infant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of noninvasive techniques to study cerebral metabolism in the human brain.
the development and use of non-invasive techniques to measure brain function in newborn infants.
the development and application of noninvasive methods for the assessment of cerebral oxidative metabolic function in the human neonate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
NIRS and MMR are complementary and that both are important tools in the assessment and management of the newborn infant with perinatal asphxia.

the brain in the newborn is not a simple organ, but a complex organ, with different regions, different cell types, and a complex metabolic network, which has to be understood in order to develop new therapeutic strategies.
the use of NIRS and MIRS is a very promising approach in the field of perinatal brain research.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NIRS is a useful tool to measure cerebral oxygenation and haemodynamics in newborn infants.

NIRS and MMR spectroscopy are noninvasive, safe and reliable methods of monitoring cerebral oxygenation and metabolism in the neonatal period and are of great value in the diagnosis of hypoxia-ischemia and in the evaluation of new therapies for this condition.
NIRS and MIRS are complementary methods for the noninvasive assessment of the cerebral energy state in the human newborn.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of NIRS and MMR is a powerful non-invasive technique for the study of brain function and dysfunction in the newborn.
MRS and NIRS provide unique information on cerebral metabolism in newborn infants and that these techniques are likely to play an increasing role in clinical studies of the newborn brain.
NIRS and MMR are complementary techniques for assessing cerebral oxidative metabolism and for guiding the introduction of new therapeutic approaches to the management of perinatal asphysia.
